section_summary: This section concludes an FBI account of Japanese commercial, intelligence, and clandestine communications networks operating principally in Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. It then documents suspected Japanese interests in an Ecuadorian oil concession, warnings about Spanish newspaper correspondents allegedly collecting intelligence for Japan, and Japanese efforts to obtain American scientific and technical publications. The final pages begin a Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service report on Japanese wartime politics, propaganda, mobilization, and Greater East Asia policy.

subfiles.title: Japanese commercial and espionage networks in Chile, Argentina, and Brazil (continuation)
subfiles.about: Continuation of an investigation into Japanese commercial firms, clandestine communications, mail drops, and intelligence activity in South America.
subfiles.summary: The report describes the Compañía Chilena Oriental's collection of detailed American economic and war-production information, its plans to evacuate staff and destroy records after Pearl Harbor, and its movement of funds through lawyers, legations, and affiliated firms. It reconstructs coded communications linking Santiago and Buenos Aires through aliases and intermediaries associated with Casa Taibo, Iwai, and other Japanese companies. The report also follows related contacts in Brazil, including Alberto Telles, Ary de Andrade Figueira, Suetaka Hayao, and alleged Nazi intelligence chief Friedrich Zedlitz, and notes requests from Tokyo for information on American air defenses and forces in China.

subfiles.title: Japanese Activities in Argentina
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Assistant Secretary of State Adolf A. Berle Jr.
subfiles.about: Reports a Chilean courier's proposed Japanese-directed journey to inspect strategic sites in Bolivia, Peru, and Ecuador.
subfiles.summary: A confidential source reported that Carlos Santa Cruz planned a two-month journey for the Japanese Embassy in Buenos Aires to observe strategic areas, particularly oil bases, in Bolivia, Peru, and Ecuador. He was also expected to carry concealed letters to Peru, while correspondence from his mother in Santiago was allegedly intended for Japanese recipients in Buenos Aires. The information had been supplied to the American Embassy in Buenos Aires.

subfiles.title: Transmittal: Compañía Minero Petrolera del Pacífico—Ecuador
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Transmits an enclosed memorandum concerning suspected hostile foreign interests in an Ecuadorian oil company.
subfiles.summary: Hoover forwards supplementary information on the Compañía Minero Petrolera del Pacífico and promises to transmit further findings from the continuing inquiry. The information came from a reliable confidential source and had also been shared with the American embassies in Quito and Bogotá and with the Office of Exports.

subfiles.title: Compañía Minero Petrolera del Pacífico
subfiles.about: Investigates whether Japanese capital or governmental interests were concealed in an Ecuadorian petroleum concession employing Japanese technicians.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum examines the company's proposed sale, its financing, and the hiring of Japanese geologists and topographers through the Japanese minister to Peru. Although company officials denied Japanese ownership and opened their records, the inquiry notes unexplained Colombian financing, proposed guarantees to Japan, espionage allegations, and disputed claims surrounding the technicians' contracts. It reviews the firm's capitalization, shareholder and concession transactions, the conflicting allegations of Manuel Torres Peralta, and the possible role of Felix Castillo Marino. The concluding pages reproduce a release terminating the employment contracts of six Japanese technicians after war with the United States made their work impossible.

subfiles.title: Secret airgram to Buenos Aires concerning Spanish newspaper correspondents
subfiles.about: Orders discreet surveillance of Spanish correspondents suspected of conducting intelligence work for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department reports that correspondents for El Alcázar, A.B.C., and Información may travel from Spain to Buenos Aires while ostensibly reporting from major South American capitals. Their actual mission was believed to include sending secret intelligence dispatches for the Japanese government and forwarding publications through the Hispanidad headquarters in Madrid. The embassy was instructed to avoid overt action, watch for their arrival, and report developments by secret airgram.

subfiles.title: Secret airgram to Santiago concerning Spanish newspaper correspondents
subfiles.about: Directs the Santiago embassy to monitor suspected Japanese intelligence operatives posing as Spanish correspondents.
subfiles.summary: The Department warns that correspondents for three Spanish newspapers may use assignments in Buenos Aires, Rio de Janeiro, and Santiago as cover for intelligence collection serving Japan. They were also expected to send newspapers and magazines to Madrid for onward transmission to Japanese authorities. Santiago was asked to conduct discreet surveillance and report useful developments secretly to the Chief of the Division of Foreign Activity Correlation.

subfiles.title: Secret airgram to Rio de Janeiro concerning Spanish newspaper correspondents
subfiles.about: Directs surveillance of Spanish newspaper correspondents believed to be gathering intelligence for Japan.
subfiles.summary: This parallel warning says correspondents for El Alcázar, A.B.C., and Información might depart Spain for Buenos Aires and operate in Buenos Aires, Rio de Janeiro, and Santiago. Their suspected real duties were secret reporting for Japan and collection of publications for transmission through Madrid. The embassy was cautioned against revealing that the United States knew of the plan and was told to report developments by secret airgram.

subfiles.title: Lysette Telles—Japsa Case
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Updates the State Department on Lysette and Alberto Telles and their connection to the broader Japsa espionage investigation.
subfiles.summary: Lysette Telles, formerly employed by the Japanese Embassy in Rio de Janeiro, was found working in a non-confidential post at the Rubber Development Corporation. The memorandum recalls that her father Alberto received a Buenos Aires letter for Ryokichi Nagai typed on the same machine as espionage-related correspondence attributed to S. Miura. It further reports that Alberto Telles handled the affairs of a Mitsui affiliate and was believed to collect intelligence for Japan.

subfiles.title: Japanese Espionage
subfiles.from: J. Edgar Hoover, Director, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.to: Adolf A. Berle Jr., Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports that Japanese intelligence instructed South American agents to forward selected American publications to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hoover advises that the Japanese Intelligence Service had directed agents throughout South America to obtain and send to Japan publications in specified technical fields. A detailed list of the requested American publications is attached, and copies of the communication were supplied to Army and Navy intelligence recipients.

subfiles.title: List of United States publications requested by Japanese intelligence
subfiles.about: Lists American scientific, engineering, medical, military, industrial, aeronautical, and patent publications sought by Japanese agents.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure inventories journals and reference works across natural science, mathematics, physics, chemistry, medicine, agriculture, engineering, metallurgy, naval science, aeronautics, electronics, patents, and industrial standards. It also requests recent technical catalogues and literature concerning DuPont products and Pfaudler glass-lined chemical equipment. The breadth of the list indicates systematic Japanese collection of open-source American scientific and industrial information.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of “Japan's Menace to the Americas”
subfiles.from: Russell Pierce, Assistant Director, Radio Division, Coordinator of Inter-American Affairs
subfiles.about: Forwards six additional copies of Mr. Naft's report “Japan's Menace to the Americas.”
subfiles.summary: Russell Pierce responds to a telephone request from John Draier by sending six additional copies of a report titled “Japan's Menace to the Americas.” The report itself is not reproduced on this page.

subfiles.title: Radio Report on the Far East, Number 25
subfiles.from: Foreign Broadcast Intelligence Service, Federal Communications Commission
subfiles.about: Analyzes monitored Japanese broadcasts concerning domestic wartime mobilization, propaganda, and policy in Greater East Asia.
subfiles.summary: The report explains the limitations and propaganda character of Japanese broadcasts, then surveys the Fourth Central Cooperative Council meeting and speeches by Tojo and other officials stressing the gravity of the war, increased production, air power, transport, and national sacrifice. It reviews Japanese political administration, Diet organization, budgets, propaganda controls, food policy, and appointments. The final pages cover Tojo's tour of occupied and allied Asian territories, Japanese-sponsored political and cultural organizations, missions, conferences, and programs intended to consolidate the Greater East Asia order. The report continues beyond the end of this section.
